lessons.title: Comparing Like Fractions (page 96)

mcqs.q: Umar colours 1/4 of a circle and Mariam colours 3/4 of the same size circle. Who coloured more?
mcqs.why: Both fractions have denominator 4, and numerator 3 is greater than numerator 1, so 3/4 is greater than 1/4 and Mariam coloured more.

mcqs.q: If fractions have the same denominators, which fraction is greater?
options: The one with the smaller numerator
The one with the greater numerator
mcqs.why: The notes say with the same denominators, the greater the numerator the greater the fraction, and the smaller the numerator the smaller the fraction.

mcqs.q: Compare 3/4 and 1/4. Which sign is correct?
mcqs.why: Denominators are both 4, so compare numerators: 3 is greater than 1, therefore 3/4 is greater than 1/4, written 3/4 > 1/4.

mcqs.q: Compare 2/7 and 4/7. Which sign is correct?
mcqs.why: Denominators are both 7, so compare numerators: 2 is smaller than 4, therefore 2/7 is smaller than 4/7, written 2/7 < 4/7.

mcqs.q: Compare 4/5 and 4/5. Which sign is correct?
mcqs.why: Both fractions are 4/5 with equal numerators and equal denominators, so they are equal and we write 4/5 = 4/5.

mcqs.q: Which fraction is greater: 5/8 or 2/8?
mcqs.why: Denominators are both 8, so compare numerators: 5 is greater than 2, therefore 5/8 is greater than 2/8.

mcqs.q: Which fraction is smaller: 3/8 or 6/8?
mcqs.why: Denominators are both 8, so compare numerators: 3 is smaller than 6, therefore 3/8 is smaller than 6/8.

mcqs.q: Compare 4/10 and 3/10. Which is correct?
mcqs.why: Denominators are both 10, so compare numerators: 4 is greater than 3, therefore 4/10 is greater than 3/10.

mcqs.q: Which symbol means greater than?
mcqs.why: The symbol > means greater than, the symbol < means less than, and the symbol = means equal to, as used for comparing fractions.

mcqs.q: Compare 6/7 and 4/7. Which is correct?
mcqs.why: Denominators are both 7, so compare numerators: 6 is greater than 4, therefore 6/7 is greater than 4/7.

lessons.notes_html: Comparing fractions with the same denominators using symbols <, > and =. We can explain comparing fractions with the following example: Umar divides a circle into 4 equal parts. He colours one part of the circle (1/4). Mariam also divides a circle into 4 equal parts. She colours three parts (3/4). Who coloured more? Here (3/4) is greater than 1/4, or 3/4 > 1/4. So, Mariam coloured more parts (3/4) of the circle than Umar. If fractions have the same denominators, then greater the numerator, the greater will be the fraction and smaller the numerator, the smaller will be the fraction. Example (page 96): Write <, > or = to compare fractions of the same denominator: 1) 3/4 ___ 1/4. Solution: 3/4 > 1/4. Numerator 3 is greater than 1, i.e., 3 > 1. 2) 2/7 ___ 4/7. Solution: 2/7 < 4/7. Numerator 2 is smaller than 4, i.e., 2 < 4. 3) 4/5 ___ 4/5. Solution: 4/5 = 4/5. Numerator of both fractions are equal, i.e., 4 = 4.

lessons.title: Ordering of Fractions (page 97)

mcqs.q: What is ordering of fractions?
options: Arranging fractions in ascending and descending order
mcqs.why: The notes say fractions can be arranged in ascending and descending order, and such arrangement is called ordering of fractions.

mcqs.q: Arrange 2/6, 4/6, 1/6 and 3/6 in ascending order.
mcqs.why: Denominators are all 6, so order the numerators from smallest to greatest: 1, 2, 3, 4 gives 1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6.

mcqs.q: Arrange 1/5, 3/5, 2/5 and 4/5 in descending order.
mcqs.why: Denominators are all 5, so order the numerators from greatest to smallest: 4, 3, 2, 1 gives 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5.

mcqs.q: Compare 2/4 and 3/4. Which sign is correct?
mcqs.why: Denominators are both 4, so compare numerators: 2 is smaller than 3, therefore 2/4 is less than 3/4, written 2/4 < 3/4.

mcqs.q: Compare 4/10 and 3/10. Which sign is correct?
mcqs.why: Denominators are both 10, so compare numerators: 4 is greater than 3, therefore 4/10 is greater than 3/10.

mcqs.q: Arrange 3/4, 2/4, 1/4 and 4/4 in ascending order.
mcqs.why: Denominators are all 4, so order the numerators from smallest to greatest: 1, 2, 3, 4 gives 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.

mcqs.q: Arrange 3/10, 5/10, 2/10 and 4/10 in descending order.
mcqs.why: Denominators are all 10, so order the numerators from greatest to smallest: 5, 4, 3, 2 gives 5/10, 4/10, 3/10, 2/10.

mcqs.q: Compare 5/9 and 5/9. Which sign is correct?
mcqs.why: Both fractions are exactly 5/9, with equal numerators and equal denominators, so they are equal and we write 5/9 = 5/9.

mcqs.q: Compare 3/7 and 4/7. Which sign is correct?
mcqs.why: Denominators are both 7, so compare numerators: 3 is smaller than 4, therefore 3/7 is less than 4/7, written 3/7 < 4/7.

mcqs.q: Which fraction is the smallest: 3/11, 6/11, 5/11 or 4/11?
mcqs.why: Denominators are all 11, so the smallest numerator gives the smallest fraction: 3 is smallest, so 3/11 is the smallest.

lessons.notes_html:
Fractions can be arranged in ascending and descending order. Such arrangement is called ordering of fractions. Example (page 97): Arrange the following fractions in ascending order: 2/6, 4/6, 1/6, 3/6. Solution: 1/6 < 2/6 < 3/6 < 4/6. Ascending order: 1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6. Example (page 97): Arrange the following in descending order: 1/5, 3/5, 2/5, 4/5. Solution: 4/5 > 3/5 > 2/5 > 1/5. Descending order: 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5.

lessons.title: Addition of Fractions (page 99)

mcqs.q: How do we add like fractions?
options: Add the numerators and keep the denominator
Keep the numerators and add denominators
mcqs.why: For like fractions we add the numerators and keep the same denominator, as in 3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8 where 3 + 4 = 7.
Denominators are the same, so add the numerators: 3 + 4 = 7 and keep the denominator 8, giving 7/8.
Denominators are the same, so add the numerators: 3 + 1 = 4 and keep the denominator 5, giving 4/5.
Denominators are the same, so add the numerators: 3 + 5 = 8 and keep the denominator 9, giving 8/9.
Add the numerators: 1 + 2 = 3 and keep the denominator 3, giving 3/3, and 3/3 makes one whole, which is 1.
Add the numerators: 6 + 7 = 13 and keep the denominator 13, giving 13/13, and 13/13 makes one whole, which is 1.

mcqs.q: What is the first step when adding unlike fractions?
mcqs.why: The notes show that for unlike fractions we first make the denominators same, then add the numerators and keep that denominator.
Make denominators same: 2/6 = 4/12. Then add numerators: 4 + 3 = 7 and keep denominator 12, giving 7/12.
Make denominators same: 2/3 = 4/6. Then add numerators: 4 + 3 = 7 and keep denominator 6, giving 7/6.
Make denominators same: 1/2 = 4/8. Then add numerators: 4 + 5 = 9 and keep denominator 8, giving 9/8.

lessons.notes_html:
Addition of Like Fractions: Example (page 99): Add 3/8 + 4/8. Solution: 3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8 (add the numerators, keep the denominator). Addition of Unlike Fractions: Example (page 99): Add 2/6 + 3/12. Solution: First make the denominators same: (2 x 2)/(6 x 2) + 3/12 = 4/12 + 3/12. Now add the numerators as follows: (4 + 3)/12 = 7/12.

lessons.title: Subtraction of Fractions (page 101)

mcqs.q: How do we subtract like fractions?
options: Subtract the numerators and keep the denominator
Add the numerators and keep the denominator
mcqs.why: For like fractions we subtract the numerators and keep the same denominator, as in 7/8 - 3/8 = 4/8 where 7 - 3 = 4.

mcqs.q: Subtract 7/8 - 3/8.
mcqs.why: Denominators are the same, so subtract the numerators: 7 - 3 = 4 and keep the denominator 8, giving 4/8.

mcqs.q: Subtract 2/3 - 1/3.
mcqs.why: Denominators are the same, so subtract the numerators: 2 - 1 = 1 and keep the denominator 3, giving 1/3.

mcqs.q: Subtract 5/6 - 3/6.
mcqs.why: Denominators are the same, so subtract the numerators: 5 - 3 = 2 and keep the denominator 6, giving 2/6.

mcqs.q: Subtract 8/10 - 7/10.
mcqs.why: Denominators are the same, so subtract the numerators: 8 - 7 = 1 and keep the denominator 10, giving 1/10.

mcqs.q: Subtract 9/16 - 7/16.
mcqs.why: Denominators are the same, so subtract the numerators: 9 - 7 = 2 and keep the denominator 16, giving 2/16.

mcqs.q: What is the first step when subtracting unlike fractions?
mcqs.why: The notes show that for unlike fractions we first make the denominators same, then subtract the numerators and keep that denominator.

mcqs.q: Subtract 9/12 - 3/6.
mcqs.why: Make denominators same: 3/6 = 6/12. Then subtract numerators: 9 - 6 = 3 and keep denominator 12, giving 3/12.

mcqs.q: Subtract 5/9 - 1/3.
mcqs.why: Make denominators same: 1/3 = 3/9. Then subtract numerators: 5 - 3 = 2 and keep denominator 9, giving 2/9.

mcqs.q: Subtract 7/12 - 3/6.
mcqs.why: Make denominators same: 3/6 = 6/12. Then subtract numerators: 7 - 6 = 1 and keep denominator 12, giving 1/12.

lessons.title: Hundredths (page 102)

mcqs.q: One whole is divided into 100 equal parts. What is 1 part called?
mcqs.why: Dividing one whole into 100 equal parts makes each part 1/100, which is called 1 hundredth in the notes.

mcqs.q: How many hundredths make 1 whole?
mcqs.why: The notes say 1 whole = 100 hundredths, because the whole is divided into 100 equal parts and all 100 parts make the whole.

mcqs.q: A square has 32 shaded parts out of 100 parts in all. What fraction is shaded?
mcqs.why: Shaded parts go on top and total parts below: 32 shaded parts out of 100 parts in all gives 32/100, which is 32 hundredths.

mcqs.q: How is 32/100 written in a place value chart?
mcqs.why: The notes show 32/100 as 32 hundredths: the 3 goes in the Tenths place and the 2 in the Hundredths place, with Ones 0.

mcqs.q: Write 34/100 in words.
mcqs.why: The denominator 100 means hundredths, and the numerator is 34, so 34/100 is read as thirty-four hundredths.

mcqs.q: Write 5/100 in words.
mcqs.why: The denominator 100 means hundredths, and the numerator is 5, so 5/100 is read as five hundredths.

mcqs.q: Write fifty seven hundredths as a fraction.
mcqs.why: Fifty seven tells the numerator 57 and hundredths tells the denominator 100, so fifty seven hundredths is written as 57/100.

mcqs.q: Write sixteen hundredths as a fraction.
mcqs.why: Sixteen tells the numerator 16 and hundredths tells the denominator 100, so sixteen hundredths is written as 16/100.

mcqs.q: Show 1 25/100 in hundredths. How many hundredths is it in all?
mcqs.why: One whole is 100 hundredths, so 1 25/100 = 100 hundredths + 25 hundredths = 125 hundredths in all.

mcqs.q: Write 97/100 in words.
mcqs.why: The numerator is 97 and the denominator 100 means hundredths, so 97/100 is read as ninety-seven hundredths.

lessons.notes_html:
Divide one whole into 100 equal parts: 1 part = 1/100 = 1 hundredth. 1 whole = 100 hundredths. We can write it in a place value chart as: Ones 0, Tenths 0, Hundredths 1. We can also show it on a number line as: 0, 1/100, 5/100, 10/100. Example (page 102): What are the hundredths for the shaded parts of a square? 32/100: 32 shaded parts, 100 parts in all = 32 hundredths. We can write it in a place value chart as: Ones 0, Tenths 3, Hundredths 2. On the number line: 30/100, 32/100, 35/100, 40/100. Show in hundredths 1 25/100 = 1 25/100 = 1 whole + 25 hundredths = 100 hundredths + 25 hundredths = 125 hundredths.

lessons.title: Identifying Tenths (page 104)

mcqs.q: A strip is divided into 10 equal parts and 2 parts are shaded. What are the shaded parts?
mcqs.why: Two shaded parts out of 10 equal parts are 2 tenths, written as the fraction 2/10 and as the decimal number 0.2.

mcqs.q: How many tenths make 1 whole?
mcqs.why: The notes say 1 whole = 10 tenths, because the whole is divided into 10 equal parts and all 10 parts make the whole.

mcqs.q: What is 2/10 written as a decimal number?
mcqs.why: The fraction 2/10 means 2 tenths. In the place value chart Ones is 0 and Tenths is 2, so the decimal number is 0.2.

mcqs.q: What does a decimal point do?
options: It shows the end of a number
It separates a whole number from a fractional part
mcqs.why: The notes say a decimal point separates a whole number from a fractional part of a number, and the point is called the decimal point.

mcqs.q: A circle has 3 shaded parts out of 10 parts in all. What is the decimal number?
mcqs.why: Three shaded parts out of 10 are 3 tenths, written 3/10. In the chart Ones is 0 and Tenths is 3, so the decimal is 0.3.

mcqs.q: How is 0.2 read?
mcqs.why: The notes say 0.2 is read as zero point two, because the digit 2 is in the Tenths place after the decimal point.

mcqs.q: How is 0.2 written in a place value chart?
mcqs.why: For 0.2 there is no whole part, so Ones is 0, and the 2 tenths go in the Tenths place, giving Ones 0 and Tenths 2.

mcqs.q: Write 3 tenths as a fraction.
mcqs.why: Tenths means the whole is divided into 10 parts, so 3 tenths is written with 3 on top and 10 below, giving 3/10.

mcqs.q: What is a number like 0.2, with a decimal point, called?
mcqs.why: The notes call 0.2 a decimal number. It has a digit to the right of the decimal point, showing tenths of a whole.

mcqs.q: On the number line in the notes, 0.5 stands for how many tenths?
mcqs.why: The decimal 0.5 has 5 in the Tenths place, so it stands for 5 tenths, which is written as the fraction 5/10.

lessons.notes_html: We divide a strip into 10 equal parts. 2 shaded parts = 2 tenths = 2/10 = 0.2. 1 whole = 10 tenths. We can write it in a place value chart as: Ones 0, Tenths 2. It is read as 'zero point two'. We call it decimal number. The point is called decimal point. We can also show 0.2 on a number line as: 0, 0.2, 0.5, 1. It is also read as two tenths of a whole. So, the decimal number is 0.2. A decimal number can have one or more digits to the right of the decimal point. Example (page 104): What is the decimal number for the shaded parts of a circle? 3/10: 3 shaded parts, 10 parts in all = 3 tenths = 0.3. In the place value chart: Ones 0, Tenths 3. It is read as three tenths. So, the decimal number is 0.3. Remember: A decimal point separates a whole number from a fractional part of a number.

lessons.title: Dividing single digit numbers and quantities by ten (page 105)

mcqs.q: Express 5/10 as a decimal number.
mcqs.why: The fraction 5/10 means 5 tenths. Write 0 in the Ones place and 5 in the Tenths place, giving the decimal number 0.5.

mcqs.q: Express 7/10 as a decimal number.
mcqs.why: The fraction 7/10 means 7 tenths. Write 0 in the Ones place and 7 in the Tenths place, giving the decimal number 0.7.

mcqs.q: Express 3 2/10 as a decimal number.
mcqs.why: The whole number 3 goes before the point and 2 tenths go after it: 3 wholes and 2 tenths make the decimal number 3.2.

mcqs.q: Express 5 4/10 as a decimal number.
mcqs.why: The whole number 5 goes before the point and 4 tenths go after it: 5 wholes and 4 tenths make the decimal number 5.4.

mcqs.q: Express the decimal number 0.4 as a fraction.
mcqs.why: The decimal 0.4 has 4 in the Tenths place, so it means 4 tenths, which is written as the fraction 4/10.

mcqs.q: Express the decimal number 0.8 as a fraction.
mcqs.why: The decimal 0.8 has 8 in the Tenths place, so it means 8 tenths, which is written as the fraction 8/10.

mcqs.q: Express the decimal number 2.3 as a fraction.
mcqs.why: The decimal 2.3 means 2 wholes and 3 tenths: the 2 stays as the whole number and 3 tenths is 3/10, giving 2 3/10.

mcqs.q: Express the decimal number 4.5 as a fraction.
mcqs.why: The decimal 4.5 means 4 wholes and 5 tenths: the 4 stays as the whole number and 5 tenths is 5/10, giving 4 5/10.

mcqs.q: Show 2 4/10 in tenths. How many tenths is it in all?
mcqs.why: Each whole is 10 tenths, so 2 wholes are 20 tenths. Then 20 tenths + 4 tenths = 24 tenths, which is 2.4.

mcqs.q: Write two and five tenths as a decimal number.
mcqs.why: Two and five tenths means 2 wholes and 5 tenths: write 2 before the point and 5 after it, giving 2 5/10 = 2.5.

lessons.notes_html:
Example (page 105): Show in tenths 2 4/10. Solution: = 2 4/10 = 2 whole + 4 tenths = 20 tenths + 4 tenths = 24 tenths = 2.4. We can write it in a place value chart as: Ones 2, Tenths 4. On the number line: 2, 2.4, 2.5, 3. We read it as 2 and 4 tenths. So, the decimal number is 2.4. It is read as two point four.

lessons.title: Unit 3 Summary (page 107)

mcqs.q: What does a fraction show?
options: A whole that is never divided
A part of a whole that is divided into equal parts
Only the total number of parts
mcqs.why: The summary says a fraction shows a part of a whole that is divided into equal parts, like one part of a divided pizza.

mcqs.q: What does the numerator tell us?
options: How many parts are being used
The size of each part only
mcqs.why: The summary says the numerator tells how many parts are being used, while the total number of parts is the denominator.

mcqs.q: What is the total number of parts of an object known as?
mcqs.why: The summary says the total number of parts of an object is known as the denominator, written below the line in a fraction.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a proper fraction?
mcqs.why: In a proper fraction the numerator is smaller than its denominator. In 3/5 the numerator 3 is smaller than the denominator 5.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an improper fraction?
mcqs.why: In an improper fraction the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator. In 5/5 the numerator 5 equals the denominator 5.

mcqs.q: What are equivalent fractions?
options: Fractions with the same denominator only
Fractions that add to one whole
Fractions that are equal to each other
mcqs.why: The summary says fractions that are equal to each other are called equivalent fractions, even if their numbers look different.

mcqs.q: When we add two fractions with the same denominators, what do we do?
mcqs.why: The summary says when we add two fractions with the same denominators, we add only the numerators and keep the denominator.

mcqs.q: Add 2/5 + 1/5 using the summary rule.
mcqs.why: Denominators are the same, so add only the numerators: 2 + 1 = 3 and keep the denominator 5, giving the answer 3/5.

mcqs.q: In two fractions with the same denominator, what do we do to subtract them?
mcqs.why: The summary says in two same denominator fractions, we subtract only the numerators and keep the denominator the same.

mcqs.q: Subtract 5/8 - 2/8 using the summary rule.
mcqs.why: Denominators are the same, so subtract only the numerators: 5 - 2 = 3 and keep the denominator 8, giving the answer 3/8.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A fraction shows a part of a whole that is divided into equal parts.
  • The numerator tells how many parts are being used.
  • The total number of parts of an object is known as denominator.
  • In a proper fraction, the numerator is smaller than its denominator.
  • In an improper fraction, the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator.
  • Fractions that are equal to each other are called equivalent fractions.
  • When we add two fractions with the same denominators, we add only numerators.
  • In two same denominator fractions, we subtract only numerators.
  • Vocabulary: Fraction, numerator, denominator, proper fraction, improper fraction, equivalent fraction, decimal, tenths, hundredths.
  • This closes Unit 3 (pages 85 to 107).

lessons.title: Standard Units of Length (pages 109 to 110)

mcqs.q: What is the basic unit of length?
mcqs.why: The notes say the metre is the basic unit of length and is denoted by m.

mcqs.q: How many centimetres are there in 1 metre?
mcqs.why: Key fact from the lesson: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 metre has 100 centimetres.

mcqs.q: What is the short form for metre?
mcqs.why: The lesson says the metre is denoted by m, while cm, km and mm are other units.

mcqs.q: Which unit is used to measure long distances?
mcqs.why: The notes say long distances are measured in kilometres, not in small units.

mcqs.q: What is the length of a pencil in the lesson?
mcqs.why: The lesson gives the length of the pencil as 10 cm, measured with a centimetre ruler.

mcqs.q: What is the length of a geometry box in the lesson?
mcqs.why: The lesson gives the length of the geometry box as 7 cm, a short object in centimetres.

mcqs.q: How long is the door in the lesson example?
mcqs.why: The lesson example says the length of the door is 2 m by 1 m, measured in metres.

mcqs.q: Which tool can be used to measure length in metres?
mcqs.why: The notes say we use a metre ruler, metre rod or measuring tape to measure length.

mcqs.q: How many centimetres are there in 2 metres?
mcqs.why: Working: 1 m = 100 cm, so 2 m = 2 x 100 cm = 200 cm.

mcqs.q: Short objects are best measured in which units?
mcqs.why: The notes say we measure short objects in millimetres or centimetres, and long objects in metres.

lessons.notes_html:
Learning Outcomes

Students' Learning Outcomes (page 108): Recognise and use the standard units of length (kilometre, metre, centimetre and millimetre) to measure and record the length of different objects. Add and subtract lengths, given in the same units to solve real-world word problems. Recognise and use the standard units of mass (Kilograms, grams and milligrams) to measure and record the mass of different objects. Add and subtract mass, given in the same units to solve real-world word problems. Recognise and use the standard units of capacity (litre and millilitre) to measure and record the capacity of different objects. Read and write temperature to the nearest appropriate unit i.e., (degrees C) using pictorial representations and relating temperature scale to number line. Compare and order temperature using <, > and = signs. Add and subtract capacities given in the same units to solve real-life word problems.

We measure the length of objects using standard units of length, which are metre, kilometre, centimetre and millimetre. We measure the length of short objects in millimetres or centimetres and the length of long objects in metres. Long distances are measured in kilometres. Metre (page 109): The metre is the most appropriate unit to measure the length. It is the basic unit of length, and is denoted by 'm'. Key Fact: 1 m = 100 cm. We use metre ruler, metre rod or measuring tape as measuring scale to measure different objects. Few examples to measure the length of objects in metres (page 110): Length of door: 2 m by 1 m. Length of blackboard: 1 m by 2 m. Centimetre (page 110): A centimetre ruler is used to measure the length of short objects, and is denoted as 'cm'. Key Fact: 100 cm = 1 m. Let us observe the lengths of these objects in centimetres: The length of pencil = 10 cm. The length of geometry box = 7 cm.

lessons.notes_html:
Millimetre (page 111): A millimetre ruler is used to measure the length of very short objects, and it is denoted as 'mm'. Key Fact: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 1 centimetre = 10 millimetres. Lengths of some objects in millimetres (page 111): The length of hair clip = 20 mm. The length of leaf = 50 mm. The length of key = 30 mm. The length of button = 10 mm. Kilometre (page 111): The distance from one place to another is measured in kilometres. In short form we use 'km' for kilometre. We write 1 kilometre as '1 km'. Key Fact: 1 km = 1000 m. Example (page 111): the distance from Ziarat to Quetta is 125 km.

lessons.title: Real-World Word Problems: Length (pages 116 to 117)

mcqs.q: Nadia had 84 cm of red ribbon and 56 cm of blue ribbon. How much ribbon did she have in all?
mcqs.why: In all means add: red 84 cm + blue 56 cm = 140 cm, so she had 140 cm in all.

mcqs.q: Arif bought 75 m of red carpet and 68 m of blue carpet. What is the total length?
mcqs.why: Total means add: 75 m + 68 m = 143 m, so the total length of carpet is 143 m.

mcqs.q: The Faisal Masjid minarets are 90 m and Badshahi Masjid minarets are 70 m. What is their total height?
mcqs.why: Total means add: 90 m + 70 m = 160 m, so the total height is 160 m.

mcqs.q: Tanveer drove 687 km from Quetta to Karachi and 622 km from Karachi to Gwadar. What is the total distance?
mcqs.why: Total means add: 687 km + 622 km = 1309 km, so he travelled 1309 km in total.

mcqs.q: A train covered 858 km from A to B and 763 km from B to C. What is the total distance from A to C?
mcqs.why: Total means add: 858 km + 763 km = 1621 km, so the train covered 1621 km.

mcqs.q: The red building is 52 m high and the gray building is 38 m high. What is the difference in height?
mcqs.why: Difference means subtract: 52 m - 38 m = 14 m, so the difference is 14 m.

mcqs.q: A 200 cm cloth is cut into two pieces. One piece is 155 cm. How long is the other piece?
mcqs.why: Other piece = whole - one piece: 200 cm - 155 cm = 45 cm.

mcqs.q: Two roads are 865 km and 468 km long. What is the difference between their lengths?
mcqs.why: Difference means subtract: 865 km - 468 km = 397 km.

mcqs.q: Quetta to Islamabad is 896 km and Quetta to Zhob is 335 km. How far is Zhob from Islamabad?
mcqs.why: Zhob to Islamabad = 896 km - 335 km = 561 km, subtracting the first part.

mcqs.q: Sana's house is 12 km from school. Zara's house is 8 km farther. How far is Zara's house from school?
mcqs.why: Farther means add: 12 km + 8 km = 20 km, so Zara's house is 20 km from school.

lessons.notes_html:
Real-World Word Problems (page 116): (i) Nadia had 84 cm of red ribbon and 56 cm of blue ribbon. How much ribbon did she have in all?

Step 1: Red ribbon = 84 cm.

Step 2: Blue ribbon = 56 cm.

Step 3: In all means add: 84 + 56.

Step 4: 84 + 56 = 140.

Answer: 140 cm

Real-World Word Problems (page 116): (ii) Arif bought 75 m of red carpet and 68 m of blue carpets. What is the total length of carpet bought by Arif?

Step 1: Red carpet = 75 m.

Step 2: Blue carpet = 68 m.

Step 3: Total means add: 75 + 68.

Step 4: 75 + 68 = 143.

lessons.title: Standard Units of Mass (pages 118 to 119)

mcqs.q: Which unit is used to measure the mass of heavy objects?
mcqs.why: The lesson says we measure the mass of heavy objects in kilograms, denoted kg.

mcqs.q: How many grams are there in 1 kilogram?
mcqs.why: Key fact from the lesson: 1 kg = 1000 g, so 1 kilogram equals 1000 grams.

mcqs.q: How many milligrams are there in 1 gram?
mcqs.why: Key fact from the lesson: 1000 mg = 1 g, so 1 gram equals 1000 milligrams.

lessons.notes_html:
Standard Units of Mass (page 118): We measure the mass of an object using standard units such as kilograms, grams and milligrams. Kilogram (page 118): We measure the mass of heavy objects in kilograms. It is denoted 'kg'. Some iron masses of kilograms are: 1 kg, 2 kg, 3 kg, 4 kg, 5 kg. Some examples of mass of objects in kilograms (page 118): (i) Weight of Pumpkin is 2 kg. (ii) Weight of Wheat is 10 kg. Gram (page 118): We measure the mass of light objects in grams. In short form, it is denoted as 'g'. Key Fact: 1 kg = 1000 g. Some examples of mass of objects in grams (page 119): (i) Weight of cherries 100 g. (ii) Weight of Coriander seeds 300 g. Milligram (page 119): We measure the mass of extremely light objects in milligrams and it is denoted as 'mg'. Key Fact: 1000 mg = 1 g. Some examples of mass of objects in milligrams (page 119): Mass of fennel seeds 200 mg. Mass of cumin seeds 500 mg.

mcqs.q: Sana has a 57 kg rice bag and Raheela has a 38 kg rice bag. What is the total mass?

mcqs.why: Total means add: 648 g + 453 g = 1101 g, so the total mass is 1101 g.

mcqs.why: Total means add: 754 g + 965 g = 1719 g, so box and chocolate together are 1719 g.

lessons.notes_html:
Standard Units of Capacity (page 124): We measure the capacity of different containers using standard units of capacity, such as litre, millilitre. Remember: The amount of liquid a container can hold is called capacity. Litre (page 124): The most appropriate unit to measure the capacity of big containers is the litre. It is denoted as 'l'. We use special types of containers to measure the quantity of liquid. Few examples of quantities of liquid hold in litres (page 124): Capacity of milk bottle = 1 l. Capacity of oil bottle = 3 l. Capacity of oil bottle = 5 l. Millilitre (page 124): We measure the capacity of small containers in millilitre and it is denoted as 'ml'. Key Fact (page 125): 1000 ml = 1 l. We use special types of containers to measure the quantity of liquid (page 125): spoon 50 ml, glass 300 ml, jug 500 ml, jug 200 ml, measure 100 ml. A few examples of liquid quantities measured in millilitres (page 125): Cooking oil 200 ml. Cold Drink 300 ml. Cough Syrup 100 ml.

lessons.title: Real-World Word Problems: Capacity (pages 127 to 128)

lessons.title: Comparing Temperature (page 132)

mcqs.q: Which sign correctly compares 30 degrees C and 50 degrees C?
mcqs.why: Working: 30 is smaller than 50, so 30 degrees C < 50 degrees C using the less-than sign.

mcqs.q: Which sign correctly compares 40 degrees C and 10 degrees C?
mcqs.why: Working: 40 is greater than 10, so 40 degrees C > 10 degrees C using the greater-than sign.

mcqs.q: Which sign correctly compares 20 degrees C and 20 degrees C?
mcqs.why: Working: both temperatures are 20, the same value, so 20 degrees C = 20 degrees C.

mcqs.q: An autumn day is 20 degrees C and a snowman day is 0 degrees C. Which comparison is correct?
mcqs.why: Working: 20 is greater than 0, so autumn day 20 degrees C > snowman day 0 degrees C.

mcqs.q: In 40 degrees C, 60 degrees C and 30 degrees C, which is the greatest?
mcqs.why: Working: compare 40, 60 and 30; 60 is the biggest number, so 60 degrees C is greatest.

mcqs.q: In 70 degrees C, 50 degrees C and 80 degrees C, which is the least?
mcqs.why: Working: compare 70, 50 and 80; 50 is the smallest number, so 50 degrees C is least.

mcqs.q: A kite-flying day is 30 degrees C and a swimming day is 40 degrees C. Which is correct?
mcqs.why: Working: 30 is smaller than 40, so the book example gives 30 degrees C < 40 degrees C.

mcqs.q: A snowy house night is 10 degrees C and a snowy mountain day is 10 degrees C. Which sign fits?
mcqs.why: Working: both readings are 10 degrees C, equal values, so the correct sign is = .

mcqs.q: In 90 degrees C, 20 degrees C and 60 degrees C, which is the greatest?
mcqs.why: Working: compare 90, 20 and 60; 90 is the biggest number, so 90 degrees C is greatest.

mcqs.q: A skiing day is 0 degrees C and a spring day is 40 degrees C. Which comparison is correct?
mcqs.why: Working: 0 is smaller than 40, so skiing day 0 degrees C < spring day 40 degrees C.

lessons.title: Ordering Temperature (page 133)

mcqs.q: Write 10, 15, 50, 30, 40 and 25 degrees C in decreasing order. Which comes first?
mcqs.why: Decreasing means biggest first: 50 > 40 > 30 > 25 > 15 > 10, so 50 degrees C is first.

mcqs.q: Write 70, 60, 90, 75, 40 and 50 degrees C in increasing order. Which comes first?
mcqs.why: Increasing means smallest first: 40 < 50 < 60 < 70 < 75 < 90, so 40 degrees C is first.

mcqs.q: Write 80, 50, 10, 40, 20 and 30 degrees C in decreasing order. Which is the correct order?
mcqs.why: Decreasing order sorts biggest to smallest: 80 > 50 > 40 > 30 > 20 > 10 degrees C.

mcqs.q: Write 70, 30, 60, 20, 90 and 40 degrees C in increasing order. Which comes last?
mcqs.why: Increasing order ends with the biggest: 20 < 30 < 40 < 60 < 70 < 90, so 90 is last.

mcqs.q: What does decreasing order mean for temperatures?
mcqs.why: The lesson decreasing example goes from biggest to smallest, using the > sign between values.

mcqs.q: Write 100, 70, 50, 90, 10 and 30 degrees C in increasing order. Which comes first?
mcqs.why: Increasing means smallest first: 10 < 30 < 50 < 70 < 90 < 100, so 10 degrees C is first.

mcqs.q: Write 90, 40, 70, 50, 60 and 30 degrees C in decreasing order. Which comes second?
mcqs.why: Decreasing order: 90 > 70 > 60 > 50 > 40 > 30, so the second value is 70 degrees C.

mcqs.q: Write 80, 30, 60, 0, 40 and 50 degrees C in increasing order. Which comes first?
mcqs.why: Increasing means smallest first: 0 < 30 < 40 < 50 < 60 < 80, so 0 degrees C is first.

mcqs.q: What does increasing order mean for temperatures?
mcqs.why: The lesson increasing example goes from smallest to biggest, using the < sign between values.

mcqs.q: Write 50, 20, 90, 70, 10 and 40 degrees C in decreasing order. Which comes last?
mcqs.why: Decreasing order ends with the smallest: 90 > 70 > 50 > 40 > 20 > 10, so 10 is last.

lessons.title: Recognizing and using a.m. and p.m. (page 139)

mcqs.q: How many hours are there in 1 day?
mcqs.why: The lesson states 1 day = 24 hours, and the day is divided into two equal parts of 12 hours each.

mcqs.q: The time from 12 o'clock midnight to 12 o'clock noon is called what?
mcqs.why: The lesson says the time from 12 o'clock midnight to 12 o'clock noon is called a.m., the before noon period.

mcqs.q: The time from 12 o'clock noon to 12 o'clock midnight is called what?
mcqs.why: The lesson says the time from 12 o'clock noon to 12 o'clock midnight is called p.m., the afternoon period.

mcqs.q: Nasir has breakfast at 7 o'clock in the morning. How is this written?
mcqs.why: Morning time is a.m., so 7 o'clock in the morning is written as 7:00 a.m., as in the lesson example.

mcqs.q: Nasir goes to sleep at 9 o'clock at night. How is this written?
mcqs.why: Night time after noon is p.m., so 9 o'clock at night is written as 9:00 p.m., as in the lesson example.

mcqs.q: What should NOT be written with 12:00 midnight and 12:00 noon?
mcqs.why: The Key Note says: Do not write a.m. and p.m. with 12:00 midnight and 12:00 noon.

mcqs.q: Six o'clock in the morning is written as what?
mcqs.why: Six o'clock is in the morning, before noon, so it is a.m. time and is written as 6:00 a.m.

mcqs.q: Five thirty in the evening is written as what?
mcqs.why: Evening is after noon, so it is p.m. time. Five thirty in the evening is written as 5:30 p.m.

mcqs.q: At sunrise the clock shows 6:00. Is it a.m. or p.m.?
mcqs.why: Sunrise happens in the morning, before noon, so the time 6:00 at sunrise is 6:00 a.m., as in the exercise.

mcqs.q: Doing homework at 4:15 is in the afternoon. How is it written?
mcqs.why: Homework at 4:15 in the afternoon is after noon, so it is p.m. time and is written as 4:15 p.m.

lessons.notes_html:
Recognizing and using a.m. and p.m. (page 139): As we know there are 24 hours in a day. We divide a day into two equal parts: The first 12-hours period of the day is known as the before noon. The next 12 hours period of the day is known as the afternoon. The time, from 12 o'clock midnight to 12 o'clock noon is called a.m. The time from 12 o'clock noon to 12 o'clock midnight is called p.m. Example: Nasir has breakfast at 7 o'clock in the morning. We can also write the time as 7:00 am. Example: Nasir goes to sleep at 9 o'clock at night. We can also write the time as 9:00 pm. Key Note: Do not write a.m. and p.m. with 12:00 midnight and 12:00 noon. 1 day = 24 hour.

Using a.m. and p.m. (page 140, already given in the book): We use a.m. and p.m to tell time from 12 hour clock. The time is five o'clock in the morning - 5:00 a.m. The time is eight o'clock in the morning - 8:00 a.m. The time is twelve fifteen in the afternoon - 12:15 p.m. The time is five o'clock in the afternoon - 5:00 p.m. The time is seven thirty in the afternoon - 7:30 p.m. NOTE - the book's words for the last row read 'nine thirty', but its clock shows 7:30 and its time box reads 7:30 p.m.; 7:30 p.m. is used and the 'nine thirty' wording is a book slip.

lessons.title: Addition of Units of Time in Hours (page 143)

mcqs.q: Add 5 hours and 7 hours.
mcqs.why: Adding in the same unit: 5 hours + 7 hours = 12 hours, as shown in the lesson example.

mcqs.q: Add 18 hours and 16 hours.
mcqs.why: Working: 18 + 16 = 34. Add the ones 8 + 6 = 14, then the tens, giving 34 hours in total.

mcqs.q: What is 25 hours + 18 hours?
mcqs.why: Working: 5 + 8 = 13, write 3 and carry 1; then 2 + 1 + 1 carried = 4, so 25 + 18 = 43 hours.

mcqs.q: What is 33 hours + 26 hours?
mcqs.why: Working: 3 + 6 = 9 in the ones place and 3 + 2 = 5 in the tens place, so 33 + 26 = 59 hours.

mcqs.q: What is 45 hours + 38 hours?
mcqs.why: Working: 5 + 8 = 13, write 3 and carry 1; then 4 + 3 + 1 carried = 8, so 45 + 38 = 83 hours.

mcqs.q: What is 78 hours + 63 hours?
mcqs.why: Working: 8 + 3 = 11, write 1 and carry 1; then 7 + 6 + 1 carried = 14, so 78 + 63 = 141 hours.

mcqs.q: Add 64 hours and 38 hours.
mcqs.why: Working: 4 + 8 = 12, write 2 and carry 1; then 6 + 3 + 1 carried = 10, so 64 + 38 = 102 hours.

mcqs.q: Add 78 hours and 54 hours.

lessons.title: Perimeter and Area (page 152)

mcqs.q: What is the perimeter of a closed figure?
options: The sum of the lengths of all its sides
The number of squares inside it
The length of only one side
mcqs.why: Perimeter is defined as the sum of the lengths of all sides of a closed figure, adding every side together.

mcqs.q: What is area?
options: The sum of all side lengths
The amount of space occupied by the surface of an object
The longest side of a figure
mcqs.why: The notes define area as the amount of space occupied by the surface of an object, counted in unit squares.

mcqs.q: A square has sides of 4 cm, 4 cm, 4 cm and 4 cm. What is its perimeter?
mcqs.why: Add all four sides step by step: 4 cm + 4 cm + 4 cm + 4 cm = 16 cm, so the perimeter is 16 cm.

mcqs.q: A rectangle has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. What is its perimeter?
mcqs.why: Add the sides in order: 3 cm + 4 cm + 3 cm + 4 cm = 14 cm, so the perimeter of the rectangle is 14 cm.

mcqs.q: An irregular figure has sides 2 m, 2 m, 1 m, 2 m, 4 m, 2 m, 1 m and 2 m. What is its perimeter?
mcqs.why: Add every side: 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 16, so the perimeter of the irregular figure is 16 m.

mcqs.q: A square on a grid covers 9 unit squares. What is its area?
mcqs.why: Area equals the number of unit squares covered. The square covers 9 squares, so its area is 9 cm squared.

mcqs.q: A rectangle on a grid covers 20 unit squares. What is its area?
mcqs.why: Area is the number of unit squares covered by the figure. Counting gives 20 squares, so the area is 20 cm squared.

mcqs.q: A rectangle is 7 cm by 4 cm. What is its perimeter?
mcqs.why: The sides are 7 cm, 4 cm, 7 cm and 4 cm. Adding: 7 + 4 + 7 + 4 = 22, so the perimeter is 22 cm.

mcqs.q: A square is 5 cm by 5 cm. What is its perimeter?
mcqs.why: The four sides are each 5 cm. Adding: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20, so the perimeter of the square is 20 cm.

mcqs.q: An irregular figure covers 13 unit squares. What is its area?
mcqs.why: Area is found by counting the unit squares the figure covers. It covers 13 squares, so the area is 13 m squared.

lessons.notes_html:
Learning Outcomes

Unit 6 Geometry - Students' Learning Outcomes (page 151): Recognise and identify the units of measurement of area and perimeter and find the perimeter and area of 2-D figures (Squares and rectangles) and irregular figures (figures covers either 1/2 or 1 square unit only) on a square grid. Differentiate and classify polygons with respect to their attributes (pentagon, hexagon, octagon and decagon). Identify and differentiate between prisms and pyramids with respect to their attributes. Describe the movement of objects (i.e., slide and rotation). Recognise point, line, ray and line segment; and draw and measure line segments. Identify the centre, radius and diameter of a circle. Recognise and identify quarter turns and identify quarter turns as right angles (and vice versa). Identify half and 3-quarter turns (clockwise and anti-clockwise) as two and three right angles respectively. Identify reflective symmetry in 2-D shapes.

Perimeter (page 152): The sum of lengths of all sides of a closed figure is called its perimeter. The perimeter is measured in units such as centimetres, metres. They are denoted as cm, m. Area (page 152): Area is the amount of space occupied by the surface of an object. It is measured in square units such as square centimetres, square metre. In short, they are denoted by cm squared and m squared.

Formula: Perimeter = sum of the lengths of all sides of a closed figure.

Formula: Area = number of unit squares covered by the figure.

Perimeter of Squares and Rectangles - Examples (page 152, already given in the book): 1. To find the perimeter of a square, we add the lengths of all its sides: Perimeter of a square = 4 cm + 4 cm + 4 cm + 4 cm = 16 cm. 2. To find the perimeter of a rectangle, we add the lengths of all its sides: Perimeter of a rectangle = 3 cm + 4 cm + 3 cm + 4 cm = 14 cm.

Perimeter of irregular figures - Example 3 (page 153, already given in the book): To find the perimeter of a irregular figure, we add the lengths of all its sides. Perimeter of an irregular figure = 2 m + 2 m + 1 m + 2 m + 4 m + 2 m + 1 m + 2 m = 16 m.

Area of Squares and Rectangle on a square grid - Examples (page 153, already given in the book): 1. To find the area of the square in cm squared: Number of squares = 9. Therefore, the area of square is 9 cm squared. 2. To find the area of the rectangle in cm squared: Number of squares = 20. Therefore, the area of the rectangle is 20 cm squared. Area of an irregular figure (page 153, already given in the book): To find the area of the irregular figure in m squared: Number of squares = 13. mcqs.q: What is a polygon?

An open figure made of lines
A closed plane figure bounded by three or more line segments
A shape with only two sides
mcqs.why: The notes define a polygon as a closed plane figure bounded by three or more line segments, so it must be closed and straight-sided.

mcqs.why: The polygon table in the notes lists a triangle as having 3 sides, the smallest number for any polygon.

mcqs.q: How many sides does an octagon have?

options: It has curved sides, not straight sides
mcqs.why: A polygon is made up of straight sides. An oval is curved and not made of straight sides, so it is not a polygon.

mcqs.q: Why is an open figure NOT a polygon?
options: A polygon must be a closed figure
mcqs.why: The notes say a polygon is a closed plane figure. An open figure is not closed, so it cannot be a polygon.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of a polygon?
mcqs.why: A pentagon is a closed figure with 5 straight sides, so it fits the definition of a polygon given in the notes.

lessons.notes_html: Classifying Polygons with respect to their attributes (page 156): Polygons are two-dimensional shapes made up of straight sides. A polygon is a closed plane figure bounded by three or more line segments. Triangles, all kinds of quadrilaterals, five sided figures, seven sided figures etc., are all examples of polygons. Example (page 156, already given in the book): Polygons: a pentagon, a triangle, and a star-shaped polygon. Not Polygons: an open figure and an oval (curved, not made of straight sides). Names of some polygons (page 156): Triangle - 3 sides. Quadrilateral - 4 sides. Pentagon - 5 sides. Hexagon - 6 sides. Octagon - 8 sides. Decagon - 10 sides.

lessons.notes_html:
Polygons (page 157): Regular polygon: A regular polygon has sides of equal length and equal angles of equal measure. Irregular polygon: An irregular polygon have sides and angles that are not all equal. Regular Polygons (pictures): a pentagon, a triangle, an octagon. Irregular Polygons (pictures): an arrow-shaped polygon, a quadrilateral with unequal sides, a scalene triangle. The name of a polygon depends upon the number of sides it has. Table: Five - Pentagon. Six - Hexagon. Eight - Octagon. Ten - Decagon.

Differentiation based on attributes (pages 157-158): Pentagon: It is a five sided figure, like the shape of given house. A regular pentagon has all 5 sides and angles of equal measure. Each angle measures 108 degrees. Hexagon: It is a six sided figure like a honey comb cell. Regular hexagon's has six sides and angles are of equal measure. Each angle measures 120 degrees. Octagon: It is an eight sided figure like a stop sign. Regular octagon's all sides and all angles are of equal measure. Each angle measures 135 degrees. Decagon: It is a ten-sided figure often used in tilling patterns. Regular decagon's all 10 sides and all angles are of equal measure. Each angle measures 144 degrees.

options: A solid with two identical parallel polygonal bases

lessons.notes_html:
Differentiating Prisms and Pyramids - Prism (page 161): A prism is a 3-D solid with two identical and parallel polygonal bases connected by rectangular or parallelogram faces. OR: A prism is a polyhedron whose top and bottom faces are identical polygons, with their corresponding parallel sides. The shape of the base or end face, describes the prism. (a) Triangular prism: A triangular prism has two equal triangular bases and three faces that are parallelogram. Examples of triangular prisms include a tent and triangular chocholate bar (like toblerone). (b) Rectangular Prism: A rectangular prism has two rectangular bases eight corners and no curved faces. A example of rectangular prism is a box. Pyramid (page 161): A pyramid is 3D solid with one polygonal base and triangular faces that meet at a single point called the vertex (or apex). OR: A three dimensional shape with a polygon-shaped base and triangular faces meeting at one vertex is called a pyramid.

Pyramids continued (page 162): (a) Triangular pyramid: A triangular pyramid has a triangular base and three triangular faces that meet at one vertex. (b) Square pyramid: A square based pyramid has a square base and four triangular faces that meet at one vertex. An example is the Egyptian pyramids. Similarities: Prism and pyramid both have polygonal bases and are types of polyhedrons (solids with flat faces). Differences: Prism is defined by having two parallel bases, while pyramid have a single base and converge to an apex.

lessons.title: Movement of Objects: Slide and Rotation (page 164)

mcqs.q: What is a slide, also called translation?
options: Moving in a straight line without rotating or changing direction

mcqs.q: What is rotation?
options: Turning around a fixed point or axis
mcqs.why: Rotation is when an object turns around a fixed point or axis, either within itself or outside of it, per the notes.

mcqs.why: The book keeps its orientation and moves straight, which the notes give as the example of a slide, or translation.

mcqs.why: The notes say a clock's hands rotate around the centre, each hand following a circular path, so this is rotation.

mcqs.q: During a slide, what happens to the shape and orientation of the object?
mcqs.why: The notes list as a characteristic of a slide that the shape and orientation of the object remain the same throughout.

options: It changes as the object moves
Every point moves the same distance straight
mcqs.why: The notes say in rotation the object changes its orientation as it moves, following a circular path around the centre.

mcqs.why: The notes explain a rotating wheel combines sliding as it moves forward and rotation as it spins, both at once.

options: In a circle around a centre
The same distance in the same direction

mcqs.why: The notes name a slide for children in parks and playgrounds as another example of slide, or translation.

lessons.notes_html:
Movement of Objects: Slide and Rotation (page 164): The movement of objects can be described in two ways: slide (translation) and rotation. Slide (Translation): When an object moves in a straight line from one position to another without rotating or changing its direction, it is called slide. Slide also called Translation. Example: Sliding a book straight across a table without tilting or turning it. Every part of the book moves in the same way, so it appear the same throughout the movement. Another example is a slide for children in parks and play grounds/areas. Characteristics: The shape and orientation of the object remain the same. Every point on the object moves the same distance in the same direction.

Rotation (Turn) (page 165): When an object turns around a fixed point or axis, either within itself or outside of it, is called rotation. For example, rotating swings for children in parks and play areas demonstrate rotation. Other examples: If a clock's hands rotates around the centre, each hand rotates in circular path. Similarly, if you rotate a spinner on its spin it turns around the fixed point but stays in one spot. Characteristics: The object changes its orientation as its moves. The points on the object follow a circular path around the centre of rotation, and distance from the center to any point on the object remains the same. Both movements can occur individually or simultaneously, depending on the motion of the object. For example, a rotating wheel combines sliding (as it moves forward) and rotation (as it spins).

Key differences (page 166): In sliding (translation) an object moves straight along a path, while in rotation, it spins around a centre or its axis. Example (page 166, already given in the book): Show slide and rotation (turn). Slide: the triangle keeps its orientation and moves straight. Rotation: the triangle turns and changes its orientation.

lessons.title: Point, Line, Ray and Line Segment (page 168)

mcqs.q: What is a point?
options: A dot fixed on a surface to show the location of a place
A line that goes on forever
The shortest distance between two places
mcqs.why: The notes define a point as a dot fixed on a paper or surface to show the location of a place, named with capital letters.

mcqs.q: How are points named?
options: With capital letters like A, B, C and D
mcqs.why: The notes say capital letters A, B, C, D etc. are used for naming a point, read as point A, point B and so on.

options: A straight path of points that goes on forever in two opposite directions
A path that stops at one end
mcqs.why: The notes define a line as a long, straight path made up of points that goes on forever in two opposite directions.

mcqs.q: What is a ray?
options: It has two endpoints and stops
It goes forever in both directions
It has one endpoint and goes forever in only one direction
mcqs.why: The notes say a ray has one end point and goes forever in only one direction, written and read as ray AB.

mcqs.q: What is a line segment AB?
options: A line going forever both ways
The shortest distance between point A and point B
mcqs.why: The notes describe the line segment AB as the shortest distance between point A and B, joining the two points.

mcqs.q: Points A and B at the ends of a line segment are called what?
options: End points of the line segment
mcqs.why: The notes say point A and B are called the end points of the line segment, bounding it at both ends.

mcqs.q: To measure segment AB, where should the 0 mark of the ruler be placed?
options: In the middle of the segment
mcqs.why: Step 1 in the notes places the ruler so the 0 mark is at point A, then point B is read against the ruler.

mcqs.q: Segment AB is measured with B at the 4 mark on the ruler. How long is AB?
mcqs.why: The notes' example reads point B at the number 4 on the ruler, so the line segment AB is 4 cm long.

mcqs.q: Segment PQ is measured with Q at the 7 mark on the ruler. How long is PQ?
mcqs.why: Following the notes' steps, point Q corresponds to the number 7 on the ruler, so segment PQ is 7 cm long.

mcqs.q: To draw a line segment LM of 5 cm, point M is marked at which ruler mark from L at 0?
mcqs.why: The notes mark point M corresponding to the number 5 mark on the ruler, giving a line segment LM that is 5 cm long.

lessons.notes_html:
Point, Line, Ray and Line Segment (page 168): Point: A dot fixed on a paper or any surface to show the location of a place is an example of a point (Fig.1). The capital letters A, B, C, D etc. are used for naming the point (Fig.2). We read these points as point A, point B, point C and point D. Line: A line extends in two opposite directions without end. In other words, A line is a long, straight path made up of points that goes on forever in two opposite directions. For example, Fig.3. It is written as: line AB and read as: line AB. Ray: It has one end point and goes forever in only one direction. OR: If we extend a line segment from one end in a particular direction and put an arrow as shown in Fig.4. It is written as ray AB and read as ray AB.

Line Segment (page 169): Look at the (Fig.1), which is the shortest distance between point A and B. This shortest distance is shown here by a line segment AB. Let us mark two points A and B on a paper (fig.2). Join two point A and B, then get a line segment AB (fig.3). It is written as: line segment AB and read as: line segment AB. The point A and B are called the end points of line segment. Remember - Lines and Lines Segments: A line segment join two points on a line. In the world of maths, a line itself goes on forever in two opposite direction, but in everyday life, most people describe a line segment as a line too.

Measuring a line segment (pages 169-170): Step 1: The ruler is placed in such a way along the line segment AB that the 0 mark of the ruler should at be point A. Step 2: The point B corresponds to the number 4 on the ruler. Step 3: The line segment of AB is 4 cm long (fig.a). Measuring PQ: Step 1: The ruler is placed in such a way along the line segment PQ that the '0' mark of the ruler should be at the point P. Step 2: The point Q corresponds to the number 7 on the ruler. Step 3: The line segment of PQ is 7 cm long (fig.b). Drawing a line segment (page 170): Let us draw a line segment whose length is 5 cm. Steps to be followed: 1. Mark a point L and put the ruler so that its 0 mark coincides with L. (The remaining drawing steps continue on page 171.)

Drawing a line segment continued (page 171): 2. Mark another point M corresponding to the number 5 mark on the ruler. 3. Put your pencil at L and move it along the edge of the ruler till you reach the point M. Remove the ruler. The line segment LM is 5 cm long.

lessons.title: Centre, Radius and Diameter of a Circle (page 173)

mcqs.q: What is a circle?
options: A round shape enclosed by a curved line, with no corners and no sides
mcqs.why: The notes define a circle as a round shape enclosed by a curved line, and it has no corners (vertices) and no sides.

mcqs.q: What is the centre of a circle?
options: Point O inside the circle, always the same distance from all points on the boundary
The longest line in the circle
mcqs.why: The notes say the centre is point O inside the circle, always at the same distance from all points on the boundary.

mcqs.q: What is the radius of a circle?
options: The distance from the centre O to a point on the circle, like OB
A line through the centre joining two boundary points
mcqs.why: The notes define the radius as the distance from centre O to a point such as B on the circle, written as OB or AO.

mcqs.q: What is the diameter of a circle?
options: A line segment through the centre joining two points on the circle, like AB
mcqs.why: The notes say the line segment AB is the diameter, and the diameter must pass through the centre of the circle.

mcqs.q: How is the diameter related to the radius?
options: Diameter is three times the radius
mcqs.why: The key note states the diameter of a circle is twice its radius, written as Diameter = 2 times radius.

mcqs.q: If a radius is 4 cm, what is the diameter?
mcqs.why: Diameter is twice the radius. Working: 2 x 4 cm = 8 cm, so the diameter of this circle is 8 cm.

mcqs.q: If a radius is 5 cm, what is the diameter?
mcqs.why: Diameter is twice the radius. Working: 2 x 5 cm = 10 cm, so the diameter of this circle is 10 cm.

mcqs.q: What is the plural of radius?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that the plural of radius is radii, used when a circle has more than one radius.

mcqs.q: In a circle with diameter PR through centre Q, what are the radii?
mcqs.why: Radii go from the centre Q to the boundary, so QP and QR are the radii, while PR is the whole diameter.

mcqs.q: In a circle with diameter XZ through centre Y, what is the centre?
mcqs.why: The diameter XZ passes through centre Y, so Y is the centre, and YX and YZ are the radii of that circle.

lessons.notes_html:
Centre, Radius and Diameter of a Circle (page 173): Circle: A circle is a round shape enclosed by a curved line. It has no corners (vertices) and no sides. Centre of the circle: The centre of a circle is a 'point O' inside the circle that is always at the same distance from all points on the boundary of the circle. Radius of the circle: The distance from centre 'O' to the point B is called the radius of the circle. Symbolically, it is written as OB or AO. Diameter of the circle: The line segment AB is known as diameter. The diameter must pass through the centre of the circle. We can express symbolically diameter as AB. Key Note: Diameter of a circle is twice of its radius i.e. Diameter = 2 times radius. Plural of radius is radii.

lessons.title: Quarter Turn and Quarter Turn as Right Angle (page 175)

mcqs.q: How many degrees is a quarter turn?
mcqs.why: The notes say a quarter turn occurs when an object rotates by 90 degrees, one-fourth of a full 360 degree rotation.

mcqs.q: A quarter turn is equal to how many right angles?
mcqs.why: A quarter turn creates a right angle of 90 degrees, so a quarter turn is equivalent to one right angle.

mcqs.q: What shape does a right angle make when two lines meet?
mcqs.why: The notes say a right angle is formed when two lines or sides meet to make an L shape, measuring 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: The minute hand of a clock moves from 12 to 3. What turn is this?
mcqs.why: The notes' clock example says moving from 12 to 3 is a quarter turn of 90 degrees clockwise, forming a right angle.

mcqs.q: An arrow pointing right makes a quarter turn clockwise. Which way does it point now?
mcqs.why: Turning 90 degrees clockwise from pointing right moves the arrow to point down, as shown in the exercise.

mcqs.q: An arrow pointing down makes a quarter turn anti-clockwise. Which way does it point now?
mcqs.why: Turning 90 degrees anti-clockwise from pointing down moves the arrow to point right, as in the anti-clockwise exercise.

mcqs.q: A pencil turned upside down, end to end, is what kind of turn?
options: Not a quarter turn; it is a half turn of 180 degrees
mcqs.why: The pencil is flipped end to end, which is a half turn of 180 degrees, not a 90 degree quarter turn.

mcqs.q: A letter F changed into a backwards F is what?
options: Not a quarter turn; it is a mirror flip, not a rotation
mcqs.why: The backwards F is a mirror image, a flip, not a rotation, so the notes mark it as not a quarter turn.

mcqs.q: Standing still and turning 90 degrees to face your side is called what?
mcqs.why: The notes describe turning 90 degrees in place as a quarter turn, creating a right angle with the original direction.

mcqs.q: A full rotation is 360 degrees. A quarter turn is what fraction of it?
mcqs.why: 90 degrees is one-fourth of 360 degrees: 360 divided by 4 equals 90, which is why it is called a quarter turn.

lessons.notes_html:
Quarter Turn and Quarter Turn as Right Angle (page 175): Identifying Quarter Turn: A quarter turn occurs when an object rotates by 90 degrees in either direction i.e., clockwise or anti-clockwise. This amount of turn represents one-fourth of a full rotation (360 degrees). It is called quarter turn. Quarter Turn as Right Angle: A quarter turn creates a right angle (90 degrees). A right angle is formed when two lines or sides meet to make an 'L' shape. Therefore, if an object makes a quarter turn, it rotates by a right angle. Conversely, if you see a right angle, you can think of it as a quarter turn from the original position. Examples - Clock Hands: If the minute hand in a clock moves from 12 to 3, it makes a quarter turn (90 degrees) clockwise forming a right angle.

Turning in Place (page 176): Imagine standing still and then turning 90 degrees to face your side. This is called a quarter turn, which creates a right angle with your original direction. So, a quarter turn is a 90 degree rotation equivalent to one right angle. Identifying a quarter turn as a right angle (and vice versa) helps us visualise and measure turns more easily.

lessons.title: Half and 3 Quarter Turns as Two and Three Right Angles (page 178)

mcqs.q: How many degrees is a half turn?
mcqs.why: The notes say a half turn is a rotation of 180 degrees, which is equivalent to two right angles of 90 degrees each.

mcqs.q: A half turn is equal to how many right angles?
mcqs.why: Working: 180 degrees divided by 90 degrees equals 2, so a half turn equals two right angles, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: How many degrees is a three-quarter turn?
mcqs.why: The notes say a three-quarter turn is a rotation of 270 degrees, equivalent to three right angles of 90 degrees each.

mcqs.q: A three-quarter turn is equal to how many right angles?
mcqs.why: Working: 270 degrees divided by 90 degrees equals 3, so a three-quarter turn equals three right angles.

mcqs.q: After a half turn, a person facing forward will face which way?
mcqs.why: The notes say a half turn, clockwise or anti-clockwise, makes the person face the opposite direction from the start.

mcqs.q: Turning a book from facing up to facing down is an example of what?
mcqs.why: The notes give this book example as a half turn, changing its position by 2 right angles, which is 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: The minute hand moves from 12 to 6 clockwise. What turn is this?
mcqs.why: From 12 to 6 is two quarter turns: 90 + 90 = 180 degrees, so it is a half turn equal to 2 right angles.

mcqs.q: The minute hand moves from 12 to 9 clockwise. How many right angles does it pass?
mcqs.why: Moving 12 to 9 clockwise is a three-quarter turn of 270 degrees. Working: 270 divided by 90 equals 3 right angles.

mcqs.q: Starting facing forward, a clockwise three-quarter turn makes you face which way?
options: To the left of the original position
To the right of the original position
mcqs.why: The notes state a clockwise three-quarter turn of 270 degrees results in facing to the left of the original position.

mcqs.q: Starting facing forward, an anti-clockwise three-quarter turn makes you face which way?
options: To the right of the original position
mcqs.why: An anti-clockwise 270 degree turn from forward faces to the right; only a half turn of 180 degrees faces exactly opposite.

lessons.notes_html:
Half and 3 Quarter Turns as Two and Three Right Angles (page 178): Identifying Half Turn: A half turn is a rotation of 180 degrees, which is equivalent to two right angles (90 degrees each). Clockwise half turn: If a person or object starts facing forward, a clockwise half turn will make them face the opposite direction. Anti-clockwise half turn: An anti-clockwise half turn also results in facing the opposite direction. Example: If you turn a book from facing up to facing down, that's a half turn. You have changed its position by 2 right angles (180 degrees). Identifying three quarter turn: A three quarter turn is a rotation of 270 degrees, which is equivalent to three right angles.

Three-quarter turns (page 179): Clockwise three-quarter turn: Starting from the initial position, a clockwise three quarter turn will result in the object or person facing to the left of the original position. Anti clockwise three-quarter turn: Similarly, an anti-clockwise three quarter turn also result in facing the opposite direction. Example: If the minute hand on a clock moves from 12 to 6 in clockwise direction, it makes a two-quarter turn, which is equal 180 degrees. Hence, half turn (180 degrees) is equal to 2 right angles (90 degrees each). Similarly, if the minute hands on clock moves from 12 to 9 in the clockwise direction, it makes three-quarter turns, which equal to 270 degrees. Hence, three quarter turn (270 degrees) is equal to 3 right angles (90 degrees each). NOTE - facing after a three-quarter turn: clockwise 270 degrees from forward faces left, and anti-clockwise 270 degrees from forward faces right; only a half turn (180 degrees) faces exactly opposite, so the book's 'opposite direction' wording for the anti-clockwise case is loose and the exact facings above are used.

lessons.title: Reflective Symmetry in 2-D Shapes (page 181)

mcqs.q: What is reflective symmetry in a 2-D shape?
options: The shape can be divided into two identical halves, each a mirror image of the other
The shape has no straight sides
mcqs.why: The notes say reflective symmetry occurs when a shape divides into two identical halves along a line of symmetry, mirror images.

mcqs.q: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?
mcqs.why: Any line through the centre of a circle creates two identical halves, so a circle has infinite lines of symmetry.

mcqs.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
mcqs.why: A square has symmetry along both diagonals and the vertical and horizontal centre lines, giving 4 lines of symmetry.

mcqs.q: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle have?
mcqs.why: A rectangle has symmetry along the vertical and horizontal lines through its centre, but not diagonals: 2 lines of symmetry.

mcqs.q: How many lines of symmetry does the triangle in the notes have?
mcqs.why: The notes state the triangle has 3 lines of symmetry, each passing through a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side.

mcqs.q: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
mcqs.why: The exercise answer gives a regular hexagon 6 lines of symmetry, through opposite vertices and midpoints of opposite sides.

mcqs.q: Letter A has which line of symmetry?
mcqs.why: The notes' letter example says A has a vertical line of symmetry, dividing it into two matching mirror halves.

mcqs.q: Letter B has which line of symmetry?
mcqs.why: The notes' letter example says B has a horizontal line of symmetry, with its top and bottom halves matching as mirrors.

mcqs.q: Letter O has which lines of symmetry?
mcqs.why: The notes say O has both axes of symmetry, vertical and horizontal, each dividing it into identical mirror halves.

mcqs.q: Which of these letters is NOT symmetrical?
mcqs.why: The exercise lists T, O, B and M as symmetrical, while S has no line of symmetry, so S is not symmetrical.

lessons.notes_html:
Reflective Symmetry in 2-D Shapes (page 181): Reflective symmetry in 2-D shapes occurs when a shape can be divided into two identical halves. Along a line of symmetry, each half is a mirror image of the other. In figure, MN is the line of symmetry as it divides the shape exactly in half. NOTE - the book also states that RS is not the line of symmetry because it does not divide the shape exactly in half when folded along the line, but the figure is a rectangle and its vertical centre line RS does divide it into two identical halves; moreover page 182 states that a rectangle has symmetry along the vertical and horizontal lines through its centre. The book's RS statement is therefore incorrect for the rectangle shown, and both MN and RS are lines of symmetry of that rectangle. 1. Circle: Any line that passes through the centre of a circle creates two identical halves. Infinite Lines of Symmetry. 2. Square: A square has symmetry along both its diagonals and the vertical line through the center, and the horizontal line through the centre. 4 lines of symmetry.

Reflective Symmetry continued (page 182): 3. Rectangle: A rectangle has symmetry along the vertical and horizontal lines through its centre, but not along the diagonals. 2 lines of symmetry. 4. Triangle: Each line of symmetry passes through a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side. 3 lines of symmetry. Example (page 182, already given in the book): Look at a few letters of the English alphabets to identify the different lines of symmetry. A - Vertical line of symmetry. B - Horizontal line of symmetry. O - Both axes of symmetry.

lessons.title: Unit 6 Summary (page 184)

mcqs.q: In the unit summary, the length around a closed figure is called what?
mcqs.why: The summary key point states the length of a closed figure is called perimeter, found by adding all its side lengths.

A line going forever both ways

mcqs.q: What is a line segment?
options: Part of a line bounded by two different endpoints

mcqs.q: The radius of any circle is what part of its diameter?
mcqs.why: The summary states the radius of any circle is half of its diameter, the reverse of diameter equals twice the radius.

mcqs.q: What does the line of symmetry do to a figure?
options: Divides it into two equal halves

mcqs.q: A prism has two identical parallel bases connected by what?

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The length of a closed figure is called perimeter.
  • Classification of polygon, with respect to their attributes.
  • Prisms are defined by having two parallel bases, while pyramids have a single base and converge to an apex.
  • Polygon is a closed plane figure bounded by three or more than three line segments.
  • A regular polygons has equal sides and equal angles of measure.
  • Ray has one end point and goes on forever in one direction.
  • A line segment is a part of a line that is bounded by two different endpoints.
  • The radius of any circle is half of its diameter.
  • The line of symmetry divides a figure into two equal halves.
  • A prism has two identical parallel bases connected by flat side.
  • Area is the space occupied by any covered surface of any object.
  • Vocabulary: Perimeter, line segment, polygon, prism, point, pyramid, ray, diameter, circle, radius, centre.
  • This closes Unit 6 (pages 151 to 184).

Learning Outcomes

Unit 7: Data Handling and Probability (page 185): Students' Learning Outcomes: Represent data; read and interpret data using Carroll Diagram (including real-world problems). Describe the likelihood that everyday events will occur, using mathematical language (i.e., impossible, possible, less likely, more likely, equally likely, unlikely and certain).

Carroll Diagram (page 186): A Carroll diagram is a method used to organize or sort objects in a chart or table according to their characteristics, figures, numbers and shapes we can sort different things in Carroll diagram. Representing Data in Carroll Diagram and Interpreting it. Example: Arif has some circular and square cards in yellow and other colours. Sort these cards, represent them in Carroll diagram and interpret data. The cards are (counted from the picture): yellow circles 4, green circle 1, blue circle 1, yellow square 1, blue square 1, green square 1, brown square 1 - 10 cards in all: 6 circles and 4 squares, 5 yellow and 5 of other colours. Here we are to: Sort the cards based on shape and colour. Represent data in a Carroll diagram. Interpret data. Represent these circular and square cards in Carroll diagram according to their shapes and colours (the diagram is on page 187).

Carroll Diagram, the same data (page 187): Picture table - Yellow colour: Circles 4, Squares 2; Not Yellow colour: Circles 2 (green and brown pictured), Squares 3 (green, blue and brown pictured). Numbers table as printed - Yellow colour: Circles 4, Squares 2; Not Yellow colour: Circles 2, Squares 1. Interpret Data (as printed): 1. 4 circular cards and 2 square cards are yellow. 2. 2 circular cards and 3 square cards are not yellow. 3. 4 circular cards are yellow and 2 circle cards are not yellow. 4. 2 square cards are yellow and 3 square cards are not yellow. NOTE - the book's page 187 tables do not match its own page 186 card set, and the numbers table contradicts the picture table and the interpretation: the page 186 set has only 1 yellow square (not 2) and 3 squares that are not yellow (not 1 as the numbers table prints), and its non-yellow circles are green and blue (not green and brown as the picture table draws). The correct sort of the page 186 set is: Yellow Circles 4, Yellow Squares 1, Not Yellow Circles 2, Not Yellow Squares 3 - 10 cards in all. The book's printed values are kept above, and this corrected sort is the answer to use.

Example (page 188, already given in the book): Sort out and put the numbers in correct position in Carroll diagram. Numbers: 2, 4, 10, 12, 16, 19, 21, 24, 26, 28, 31, 36. Greater than 20 and Divisible by 4: 24, 28, 36. Less than 20 and Divisible by 4: 4, 12, 16. Greater than 20 and Not divisible by 4: 21, 26, 31. Less than 20 and Not divisible by 4: 2, 10, 19. In above Carroll diagram, we can observe that: 1. The numbers divisible by 4 less than 20 are: 4, 12, 16. 2. The numbers divisible by 4 greater than 20 are: 24, 28, 36. 3. The numbers not divisible by 4 less than 20 are: 2, 10, 19. 4. The numbers not divisible by 4 greater than 20 are: 21, 26, 31 (the book prints '29' here, but 29 is not in the number list and the table gives 31; 31 is used). 5. The number divisible by 4 are: 4, 12, 16, 24, 28, 36.

lessons.title: Probability (page 192)

mcqs.q: What is probability?
options: The chance or likelihood that an event will occur
mcqs.why: The lesson states probability is the chance or likelihood that an event will occur, and an event is something that happens.

mcqs.q: An event is certain if it does what?
mcqs.why: The lesson states an event is certain if it always happens, for example it is certain that the sun sets every evening.

mcqs.q: There are only red balls in a pot. Picking a yellow ball is what?
mcqs.why: There is no yellow ball in the pot, so picking one will never happen; the lesson calls such an event impossible.

mcqs.q: There are only red balls in a pot. Picking a red ball is what?
mcqs.why: Every ball in the pot is red, so picking a red ball always happens; the lesson calls such an event certain.

mcqs.q: A jar has 3 yellow and 3 blue balls and no red balls. Picking a red ball is what?
mcqs.why: There is no red ball in the jar at all, so picking a red ball can never happen and is impossible, as in the exercise.

mcqs.q: A jar has 6 yellow balls only. Picking a yellow ball is what?
mcqs.why: Every ball in the jar is yellow, so picking a yellow ball always happens and is certain, as in the exercise.

mcqs.q: A jar has 2 red and 5 blue balls. Picking a blue ball is what?
mcqs.why: Working: there are 5 blue balls against 2 red balls, so blue has the greater chance and picking blue is more likely.

mcqs.q: A jar has 3 yellow and 3 red balls. Picking a yellow ball is what?
mcqs.why: Working: there are 3 yellow and 3 red balls, the same number, so both colours have the same chance: equally likely.

mcqs.q: A jar has 1 blue and 6 red balls. Picking a blue ball is what?
mcqs.why: Working: there is only 1 blue ball against 6 red balls, so blue has the smaller chance and picking blue is less likely.

mcqs.q: It might rain today and the sky is cloudy. Rain today is described as what?
mcqs.why: The exercise gives this as Possible: rain can happen but does not always happen, which matches the definition of possible.

lessons.notes_html:
Probability (page 192): Probability is the chance or likelihood that an event will occur. Probability of an event can be described using words such as certain, possible, impossible, less likely, more likely, unlikely, equally likely. Certain: An event is certain if it always happen. Example: It is certain that the sun sets every evening. There are only red balls in a pot. It is certain to pick a red ball. Impossible: An event is impossible, if it will never happen. Example: It is impossible to have 13 months in a year. There are only red balls in a pot. It is impossible to pick a yellow ball. Possible: An event that can happen but does not always. Example: It is possible that I will have cereal for breakfast tomorrow. KEY NOTE: Picking a red ball from a bag is an example of an event. An event is something that happens. The probability of an event is the chance of likelihood of it happening.

Probability continued (page 193): There are six red balls and one blue ball. Then it is possible to pick red ball. Less likely: When comparing two events, one has a less chance of occurring. Example: It is less likely to see a tiger than a cat in your street. There are fewer red balls than blue balls in the pot. It is less likely to pick a red balls. More Likely: When comparing two events one has a greater chance of occurring. Example: There are more blue balls than red balls in a pot. It is more likely to pick a blue balls. Unlikely: An event that has a low chance of happening. Example: It is unlikely that it will snow in the desert. There are more yellow balls and only one red ball. It is unlikely to pick a red ball.

Probability continued (page 194): Equally Likely: Two events have the same chance of happening. Example: When you toss a coin, there is chance to get heads or tails. There are same number of yellow and blue balls, there is equal chance to pick yellow and blue balls. NOTE - the book prints 'yellow and red balls' in this last sentence, but the jar pictured holds yellow and blue balls and the sentence itself says 'yellow and blue balls'; 'blue' is used here.

Exercise (page 194): Question 1 - Write possible, impossible, certain, unlikely, more likely and less likely, equally, likely (ball counts verified at 300 dpi)

Exercise (page 194): Q1 (1) - You will pick a red ball from a jar with 3 yellow and 3 blue balls (already given)

Answer: Impossible (there is no red ball in the jar).

Exercise (page 194): Q1 (2) - You will pick a yellow ball from a jar with 6 yellow balls only

Answer: Certain (every ball in the jar is yellow).

Exercise (page 194): Q1 (3) - You will pick a blue ball from a jar with 2 red and 5 blue balls

Answer: More likely (5 blue balls against 2 red balls).

Exercise (page 194): Q1 (4) - You will pick a red ball from a jar with 5 red and 2 yellow balls

Answer: More likely (5 red balls against 2 yellow balls).

Exercise (page 194): Q1 (5) - You will pick a yellow ball from a jar with 3 yellow and 3 red balls

Answer: Equally likely (3 yellow and 3 red balls, the same chance).

Exercise (page 194): Q1 (6) - You will pick a blue ball from a jar with 1 blue and 6 red balls

Answer: Less likely (only 1 blue ball against 6 red balls; a 1-in-7 chance is also low enough to be called unlikely, but 'less likely' is the comparative word for the two colours in the jar).

Exercise (page 195): Question 1 continued - Write possible, impossible, certain, unlikely, more likely and less likely, equally, likely

Exercise (page 195): Q1 (7) - You will pick a red ball from a jar with 2 red and 5 blue balls

Answer: Less likely (only 2 red balls against 5 blue balls).

Exercise (page 195): Q1 (8) - You will pick a green ball from a jar with 5 green and 2 blue balls

Answer: More likely (5 green balls against 2 blue balls).

Exercise (page 195): Question 2 - Choose the correct answer

Exercise (page 195): Question 2 (i) - You leave your water bottle in the sun. It will feel warm. (options: Unlikely, More likely, Less likely, Certain)

Answer: Certain.

Exercise (page 195): Question 2 (ii) - You roll a number cube (1-6). Getting an even number (2,4,6) (options: More likely, Certain, equally likely, Impossible)

Answer: equally likely.

Exercise (page 195): Question 2 (iii) - It might rain today the sky is cloudy. (options: Impossible, Certain, Possible, More likely)

Answer: Possible.
